messages.subject: subset and dplyr::filter give different results when some columns are un-named
messages.subject_clean: subset and dplyr::filter give different results when some columns are un-named
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

If you read in data and only give names to some columns, then subset and filter give different results.  For example, assume the following data in file test.csv

1,11,16,21
2,12,17,22
3,13,18,23
4,14,19,24
5,15,20,25

> t  <-  read.csv("test.csv", header=FALSE)
> colnames(t) <- c("ID", "X")
> t
  ID  X NA NA
1  1 11 16 21
2  2 12 17 22
3  3 13 18 23
4  4 14 19 24
5  5 15 20 25
>
> subset(t, ID < 3)
  ID  X NA NA.1
1  1 11 16   21
2  2 12 17   22

> t %>% dplyr::filter(ID < 3)
  ID  X NA NA
1  1 11 16 16
2  2 12 17 17

filter() seems to make multiple copies of the first NA column it encounters.  Obviously it is unwise to name some columns and not others, but it would be safer to make filter() more idiot-proof like subset().

Best wishes,
Jim

ff <- function(y,x) lm(y~x)$coef[1]

ddply(.data = df,.variables = "id", plyr::summarise, int=lm(y~x)$coef[1])

but this means I would need to change the code of the rest of the project (or not use dplyr in this project).

Cheers

messages.subject_clean: mimicking ldply with dplyr/tidyr: converting a list with observations of data to a data frame
messages.body_plain:
I've never posted before so if I'm in the wrong place or am providing the wrong information please just let me know.

I love dplyr/tidyr and want to convert new work and some old work to it, from plyr/reshape2. The question below is in that spirit: I know how to do it well in plyr, and have figured out how to do it unattractively with dplyr, but I want to know if there is a way to do it well with dplyr.

I want to be able to convert a list of data to a data frame, where each list element is, conceptually, an observation in a data set. A very practical application is when data returned from an API, after conversion from JSON, is in list form like this. I can do this easily with ldply but my dplyr solution is ugly. My question is, is there a better way to do it with dplyr/tidyr?

Here is a reproducible example

# Create a list of data, where each element is an observation
obs1 <- list(x="a", value=123)
obs2 <- list(x="b", value=27)
obs3 <- list(x="c", value=99)
dlist <- list(obs1, obs2, obs3)
dlist

# I want to convert this into a data frame that looks like
goal <- data.frame(x=c("a", "b", "c"), value=c(123, 27, 99))
goal

# In the days of plyr I would do this by
df1 <- ldply(dlist, data.frame)
df1

# Here is how I have figured out how to do it with dplyr. (It produces rbind_all warnings and slight differences in column types, but neither concerns me.)
# No self-respecting analyst should accept a solution like this. This CAN'T be the best dplyr solution, can it?
df2 <- data.frame(recs=1:length(dlist)) %>%
       group_by(recs) %>%
       do(data.frame(t(unlist(dlist[.$recs])))) %>%
       ungroup() %>% select(-recs)
df2

Again, I know I can just use ldply, but I am trying to use dplyr as well as possible, and I am trying to convert to dplyr/tidyr as much as possible. Many thanks if you have a better way.

Don

messages.subject_clean: Getting dplyr's group_by output to be as clearly labeled as dlply's
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I hope I'm missing something simple regarding how dplyr labels group_by output. Below is an example that shows that the way I'm doing it, groups are labeled with [[n]] in dplyr while dlply uses clear group labels.

Thanks,
Bob

# Create some data.
gender <- sample(c("Male","Female"), 100, replace = TRUE)
treatment  <- sample(LETTERS[1:4], 100, replace = TRUE)
score  <- rnorm(100)
df <- data.frame(gender, treatment, score)
head(df)

# This uses plyr to get t.tests that compare genders
# for each treatment level. The output is clearly
# labeled by treatment (my goal).
myfun <- function(x) {
  with(x,
       t.test(score ~ gender)
  )
}
library("plyr")
dlply(df, .(treatment), myfun)
detach("package:plyr")

# Next I do the same thing using dplyr
library("dplyr")
my.t.tests <-
  df %>%
  group_by(treatment) %>%
  do(
    mod = t.test(score ~ gender, data = .)
  )

# This shows treatment name, but not results
my.t.tests

# This shows results, but not treatment name
my.t.tests[[2]]

# This assigns group name to results
# so the output is finally easy to read,
# just like output from dlply.
# Is there some simple approach to displaying
# output that I'm missing?
names(my.t.tests[[2]]) <- my.t.tests[[1]]
my.t.tests[[2]]
detach("package:dplyr")

messages.subject_clean: Which data structure, calculation between rows
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I recently started to put my data into tidy form and to use dplyr.
However, I struggle to find the best approach for my data. In
particular, I find myself converting from long to wide tables and back
with reshape2 all the time (thus leaving the tidy state for better
handling). Here, I suppose this approach is not very efficient so I
would like to ask for advice.

My data includes (reduced complexity for this thread): measurements and
simulations ("type" in the following) of several variables at/for
several places and times at several heights.

Thus, there are the following id variables:

time type place height

Now, I see two possibilities to put the actual numerical values into
this table: either every variable one column as proposed by the tidy
data approach or the melted way with two columns "variable" and "value".

First, I tried the proper approach with every variable one column. Here,
the main issue is that the heights of the variables do not overlap, e.g.
air temperature is measured at a different height than a heat flux. This
produces a lot of NA in the table (variables not measured at a certain
height). While, in principle, this is ok, it makes it hard to analyse
and extract one variable later. I have to remove all additional NA from
artificially introduced heights while keeping the NAs that are actually
in the data.

The second approach solves this. There is just one variable per row, no
additional heights added. This also makes it easier to summarize(), no
need for summarize_each(); one can just do an additional
group_by(variable). However, I have to do calculations with different
variables. Currently, I filter the corresponding rows, cast them back to
one variable per column form, do the calculations, melt it again and
rbind it to the original data set.

This melting and casting removes a lot from the elegance of dplyr. Is
there a better approach? For example, a mutate() based on rows would
remove my need to cast the variables into columns.

I hope I explained my issues sufficiently. Please ask for more details
if something is unclear.

Thanks a lot,
Sebastian

messages.subject: dplyr joins: Inconsitent behavior when matching on strings and factors
messages.subject_clean: dplyr joins: Inconsitent behavior when matching on strings and factors
messages.body_plain:
Hi All-

I recently discovered (through trial and error) that the '_join' functions will not match if one of the variables is a string and the other is a factor, but also does not produce an error message telling the user, and (at least with small datasets) will return the first match but not others.

It seems like the issue was discussed and (resolved) here: https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/issues/228.  I could be misreading it but seems as though the consensus was that all strings (factor otherwise) should be converted to charaters to avoid this issue.

A reproducible example is available here (http://rpubs.com/frank_davenport/22116 ) and included below. Can someone tell me if this is a bug or by design? If it is by design, it might help in future versions to at least have a warning message stating that matches between strings and factors will not work. Or maybe I am completely missing something?

My personal preference is to have _join behave the same as merge() where strings/factors are converted and matched automatically.

Thanks again to Hadley et al. for all the great work, and as always apologies if this already addressed elsewhere.

library(dplyr)
##
## Attaching package: 'dplyr'
##
## The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
##
##     filter, lag
##
## The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
##
##     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

##----Create Data Frames--------
df <- data.frame(
  V1 = c(rep("a",5), rep("b",5)),
  V2 = rep(c(1:5), 2),
  V3 = c(101:110),
  stringsAsFactors = TRUE
)

match <- data.frame(
  V1 = c("a", "b"),
  V2 = c(3, 4),
  V4 = c(99,99),
  stringsAsFactors = TRUE
)

inner_join(df,match) #This has the two matching records
## Joining by: c("V1", "V2")
##   V1 V2  V3 V4
## 1  a  3 103 99
## 2  b  4 109 99
left_join(match,df)
## Joining by: c("V1", "V2")
##   V1 V2 V4  V3
## 1  a  3 99 103
## 2  b  4 99 109
df$V1<-as.character(df$V1)
inner_join(df,match) #This has only 1 record, but does not give any warning
## Joining by: c("V1", "V2")
##   V1 V2  V3 V4
## 1  a  4 104 99
left_join(match,df) #This produces the same result, Why does it match on 'a' but not on 'b'?

Dear Jim,

thanks a lot for the offer to help!

I attached a simplified part of my data in pd.Rdata. The columns are:

height:   height of measurement/simulation
variable: measured/simulated variable
value:    value of the variable

Every column except value are id variables for me. Please note, that
there are more levels of every id variable in my data set, in
particular, there are more sites and types.

As you can see, the data are not in tidy form because the variables are
not in separate columns. Converting to tidy form with

dcast(pd, time+site+type+height~variable)

creates a lot of NA and makes some of the further steps much more
complicated. Note also, that there a NA or NaN already in the data set.

First steps:
- only for type=="simulation":
  * sd=sd_diff+sd_dir
  * fh=-fh
- complete data
  * al=sd/su

This is easily done with mutate() if the variables are in separate
columns. If the data are in the form as attached, it will be rather
inelegant, it seems.

Next, I need to calculate functions of different type. For example, for
variable sd, su, al and fh, the measurements at the largest height are
to be compared with the simulation values at the largest height, in
particular the RMSE is to be calculated. Note that this largest height
is different for every variable. It seems that in tidy form, it's not
straight forward to select the right height. Note also that in my case,
I have more type, all need to be compared to the measurements.

Furthermore, my data cover several days so the next step is to calculate
the average at every hour, eg the value at 12 am averaged over every 12
am value of every day. I did something like this:

pdav <- pd %>%
  mutate(hour=as.numeric(format(time, "%H"))) %>%
  select(-time) %>%
  group_by(hour, site, type, height, variable) %>%
  summarise(mean=mean(value, na.rm=TRUE), na=sum(is.na <http://is.na>(value)))

In tidy form, summarise() needs to be substituted by summarise_each().

Again, the values from the largest height should be analysed and plotted
(preferably with ggplot2)

That's basically it. It seems I need to convert parts of the data set
from one data form to another for every single step, making the code
rather hard to read. What is your advice?

Thanks a lot for your help,

Sebastian

require(dplyr)
require(lubridate)

nights <- data.frame(
  date = as.Date(ymd("2014-06-01")) + c(0, 1, 3, 4, 5),
  sleep = c(7.3, 6.9, 8.1, 7.5, 7.8)
)

date_range <- range(nights$date)
all_nights <- data.frame(date = seq(date_range[1], date_range[2], "day"))

all_nights %>%
  left_join(nights)
